_note: WhatsDaf's own English renderings of the Hebrew commentaries on Sefaria (Vilna edition). Keys are <commentary>:<amud><segment>.<comment>. Square brackets are our clarifications. Very long Tosafot are condensed and marked "In brief".
rashi:a1.1: “But if the white leprous spot stays in its place [taḥteha]”: it stood in its place, and this is analogous to association, in which the consecrated animal stands in its place. Therefore, since both [meanings] are implied, Scripture handed it over only to the Sages, who know how to say where taḥat means association and where it means desacralization.
rashi:a2.1: With regard to animals consecrated for Temple maintenance, etc. [Rashi cites the words without further comment.]
rashi:a4.1: His hand on the consecrated animal, it is non-sacred: he placed his hand on the consecrated animal and said: This is in place of this. [As for] the other, the non-sacred one, he certainly intends [the consecrated one] to become non-sacred, and it is non-sacred.
rashi:a4.2: His hand on the non-sacred animal: and he said: This is in place of this, it is association, for a blemished consecrated animal renders a substitute; and had he wanted to desacralize it, he would have placed his hand on the consecrated one.
rashi:a5.1: And he said: These are hereby in place of those: and he did not place his hand either here or there. [Rashi’s heading has the stray word “sin offering” in parentheses, marked for deletion.]
rashi:a6.1: To associate: does he intend to associate, or does he intend to desacralize? And the same dilemma could have been raised about a single [pair]; but since it wishes to raise another dilemma about two, it took up the pattern of two [here too].
rashi:a6.2: The prohibition: [of] “He shall not substitute it” (Leviticus 27:10).
rashi:a8.1: Unblemished in place of unblemished, to associate: for it is certainly impossible that one of them is not for association, since there is at least one unblemished consecrated animal among animals consecrated for the altar, and with unblemished ones we said above that it is association.
rashi:a8.2: And blemished in place of blemished, to desacralize: for one certainly cannot say [that it is] association, since “bad for bad” is not written [in the verse] so as to effect substitution.
rashi:a9.1: Or perhaps the unblemished non-sacred in place of the blemished, etc.: even though it was resolved above that one does not abandon the permitted way and perform the prohibited, there is room to ask here. Since it is impossible that he did not perform a prohibition with one of them, one may say: just as he performs a prohibition with this one, he does not mind with that one too, and it is certainly association.
rashi:a10.1: If there were three animals before him, etc.: even though I resolved that one does not abandon the permitted way and perform the prohibited, there is room to ask here, for one may say: go after the majority. Since two are perforce for association, as the two consecrated ones are unblemished and desacralization does not apply to them, the third too is association.
rashi:a12.1: The man has not been established: for three times make a presumption [ḥazaka]; twice is not a presumption. [Rashi now records a different version of the passage, which he calls] the Jerusalem version: Abaye raised a dilemma, etc. Or perhaps unblemished in place of unblemished is for association, since [the consecrated animal] is fit for sacrifice; but unblemished in place of blemished, since the blemished consecrated animal is not fit for sacrifice, he intended to desacralize. Since he wished to say one for association, etc.: that is, had it been in his mind to associate one and to desacralize one, he would have said explicitly: this one to associate and this one to desacralize. “Alike”: that is, he made both of them equal, since he did not specify; he placed his hand on both [non-sacred animals], and both are substitutes, for had it been in his mind to desacralize it he should have placed his hand on the blemished consecrated animal. Rather, if there were before him, etc.: since these two animals are for association, for he certainly associates these two non-sacred animals with that consecrated one, as one may substitute two for one, and since the consecrated one is unblemished one cannot say [it is] to desacralize, that blemished one too is for association, and he is flogged three sets of lashes. Or perhaps that blemished consecrated animal is for desacralization, and [as for] the fact that he did not place his hand on that blemished one but placed his hand on the non-sacred ones [it is no proof], for since he wished to desacralize, he should have placed it on the blemished consecrated animal. The reason it states “that whole blemished one” is to teach us that had he placed his hand on the unblemished consecrated animal that is with the blemished one, it would also be effective, as though he had placed it on the blemished one itself; and we say of that one, which can be desacralized, that he intended to desacralize, and of the unblemished one, to associate, even though he placed his hand on it, since desacralization cannot be said of it itself. Rami ramuyei [he set them opposite each other]: for example, there were three consecrated animals, one of them blemished, and three unblemished non-sacred animals, and he set them in two rows, one opposite the other (and this rami is like “it happened,” that he aligned them one opposite the other), and he placed his hand on the non-sacred ones and said: These are in place of those. Do we say that since he set one opposite one, he divided them for this reason, that he did not wish to treat the blemished one like these, that is, for association, but rather for desacralization? Or perhaps we follow his own words, and he placed his hand on the non-sacred ones and intended to associate. Another version: Or perhaps we follow the majority, and since the majority are for association, it too is for association.
rashi:a16.1: It is desacralized by Torah law: as we say in the chapter HaMenaḥot VehaNesakhim (Menaḥot 101a): “And if it be any impure animal” (Leviticus 27:11): the verse speaks of blemished animals that were redeemed.
rashi:a16.2: By rabbinic law: for by Torah law there is no exploitation for consecrated property, as it is written: “You shall not wrong one another [literally: a man his brother]” (Leviticus 25:14), and not consecrated property.
rashi:a16.3: Even required to conduct an appraisal by Torah law: Rav Ḥisda explains it below.
rashi:a17.1: If we say regarding exploitation: that he was wronged by only one-sixth.
rashi:a19.1: Nullification of a transaction: that he was wronged by more than one-sixth.
tosafot:a5.1: Rav Ashi raises a dilemma: If there were before him two animals: [Tosafot’s text reads Rav Ashi here, where ours reads Abaye.] The same dilemma could have been raised about one blemished consecrated animal and one unblemished non-sacred animal; but since the dilemmas that follow deal specifically with two animals, it took this case here too.
tosafot:a8.1: Blemished in place of blemished to desacralize, or perhaps the unblemished non-sacred in place of the blemished consecrated and the blemished non-sacred in place of the unblemished consecrated, both to associate, and he is flogged for both: This is puzzling. Why did it go to such length? It could have said briefly: blemished in place of blemished to desacralize, or perhaps this too is to associate. Rashi explained that blemished in place of blemished does not take hold, since a bad animal does not render substitution with a bad one: only good for bad or bad for good renders substitution, but not bad for bad. But this does not seem right, for we have not found this. Furthermore, on the contrary, it is implied above in the first chapter (Temurah 9a) that bad for bad does take hold, as it said there: If so, let the verse say “good for bad, or bad for it,” implying that bad for bad takes hold. However, the entire passage here implies as Rashi explained, for in the dilemma above, too, it took two unblemished non-sacred animals and did not take a blemished one. And the Ri explained that with bad for bad, too, substitution takes effect; but we have more reason to say desacralization than association, for why would he associate [sanctity with it], since he does not raise it [to anything], as this one too is not fit for sacrifice?
tosafot:a16.1: Even required to conduct an appraisal by Torah law: and it does not go out to non-sacred status until he conducts the appraisal. This is the meaning of the mishna, “it is desacralized and he must conduct an appraisal”: that is, it is desacralized when he conducts the appraisal. The reason it needed to teach “it is desacralized” is that it taught just before it expressions by which [the animals] do not go out to non-sacred status but are taken hold of in substitution, so that both this and that are sacred; so it also taught an expression of desacralization.
gershom:a1.1: It implies an expression of association, in substitution, as it is written: “But if the white leprous spot stays in its place”: that is, it stands in its place. [So too] this consecrated animal stands in its place, in its sanctity, and takes hold of another in its sanctity, as it is written: “Then both it and its substitute shall be sacred” (Leviticus 27:10).
gershom:a2.1: And it implies an expression of desacralization: that it removes it from its sanctity and this one enters in its place, as it is written: “In place of the brass” that they stole “I will bring gold” in its place. Since this is so, etc.
gershom:a3.1: Rava said: Even with animals consecrated for the altar it is an expression of desacralization, for example where the consecrated animal was blemished. Rava holds [so] because [the mishna’s] “And if the consecrated animal was blemished” also refers back to the first clause, where he said: This is hereby in place of that, for we do not find taḥat [stated] with regard to substitution. [Translated following the bracketed correction in the printed text.]
gershom:a4.1: He placed his hand on the blemished consecrated animal and said: Let this non-sacred one be in place of this consecrated one, that it be desacralized onto it: [it is] non-sacred. That is what an expression of desacralization implies: that the consecrated one goes out and this one enters in its place.
gershom:a5.1: If he placed his hand on this non-sacred one and said: Let this be in place of this, this blemished one remains consecrated and does not go out to non-sacred status, and this is its substitute.
gershom:a6.1: Do we say to associate: he means in substitution, and he is flogged two sets of lashes.
gershom:a7.1: Or perhaps wherever there is a permitted way, that he can desacralize, which involves no prohibition, would he perform the prohibition of substituting?
gershom:a8.1: Do we say, since he said unblemished in place of unblemished, it is to associate in substitution: for since both are unblemished, whichever one he places his hand on, it is taken hold of in substitution.
gershom:a9.1: And the blemished [non-sacred animal] in place of the blemished consecrated animal.
gershom:a10.1: And the blemished non-sacred animal in place of the unblemished consecrated animal, which is good for bad or bad for good, and he is flogged for both.
gershom:a11.1: And if you say: where there is some [way] to act in a permitted manner, he does not do all of it in a prohibited manner, and it is to desacralize, and he is flogged only once.
gershom:a12.1: If there were before him three consecrated animals and one of them blemished, etc.: Do we say, from [the fact that] unblemished in place of unblemished is to associate,
gershom:a13.1: the unblemished non-sacred one too [stands] in place of the blemished consecrated one, to associate, for we follow the majority?
gershom:a14.1: Or perhaps here too we say: wherever, etc. Since the man has not yet been established three times in transgressing by performing substitution, we say that he does not abandon the permitted way, and it is to desacralize.
gershom:a15.1: Rav Ashi raises a dilemma: If there were before him, etc. Another version: Abaye raises a dilemma: If there were before him, etc. Or perhaps unblemished in place of unblemished is to associate, since the unblemished consecrated animal is fit for sacrifice, and therefore substitution takes hold; but unblemished in place of the blemished consecrated animal, since the blemished one is not [fit], substitution does not take hold, and it is to desacralize.
gershom:a16.1: And if you say: here, since he should have said explicitly “one to associate and one to desacralize” and did not say so, both take hold, for he placed his hand on both of those non-sacred animals alike. For if [he meant] to desacralize, he should have placed his hand on that blemished one, as we said above: [if] he placed his hand on the consecrated animal, it is non-sacred. Since he did not place his hand on it, but on the unblemished non-sacred one, learn from this that both take hold.
gershom:a17.1: Rather, if there were before him two consecrated animals, one of them blemished, and three unblemished [non-sacred] animals, and he placed his hand on an unblemished non-sacred animal and said: These are hereby in place of those. Here he substituted two unblemished non-sacred animals for one unblemished consecrated animal, as we learned in the first chapter: One may substitute one for two, etc.
gershom:a18.1: Do we say: since these two unblemished non-sacred animals are to associate with that unblemished consecrated one, the third unblemished non-sacred one is [also] to associate, in place of the blemished consecrated one? Or perhaps it is to desacralize; and as for his not placing his hand on that unblemished consecrated one that is with the blemished one, nor on the blemished one, as the rule would have been had it been to desacralize, he did not place it there because he holds that the majority is preferable: better to place it on the majority, the three, and not on the two. But in any case his intention was to desacralize. Let it stand [unresolved]. [Rami ramuyei,] one opposite one: that is, if he set each consecrated animal opposite a non-sacred one, and those non-sacred ones are all unblemished and one consecrated animal is blemished, and he said: These are in place of those, what [is the halakha]? Do we say that since he set one opposite one, his actions prove that unblemished opposite unblemished is to associate and blemished opposite unblemished is to desacralize? Or perhaps we pay no attention to how he set them, but follow his words, for he said: These are in place of those, and this also implies that he said it about the unblemished non-sacred ones, and all of them are to associate?
gershom:a19.1: Another version: Or perhaps we follow the majority, for those non-sacred animals are the majority and on them he placed his hand, and all of them are to associate. Let it stand [unresolved].
gershom:a20.1: It is desacralized by Torah law: because when he says it in the language of substitution it does not go out to non-sacred status, but both it and its substitute are sacred; but when he said: This is hereby desacralized, he did not speak in the language of substitution.
gershom:a21.1: It is desacralized by Torah law, like disqualified consecrated animals that are redeemed; and he must conduct an appraisal, as we said above, by the words of the Sages, for by Torah law consecrated property is not subject to exploitation, as “his fellow” is written, to exclude consecrated property. With regard to what do they disagree? If we say with regard to exploitation, the law of exploitation. Another version says explicitly: that they erred by one-sixth, which is the law of exploitation, where he is obligated to return it to him; in this case would Reish Lakish say it is by Torah law? But didn’t we learn, etc.
rashi:b1.1: But didn’t Rabbi Yirmeya say: in the name of Rabbi Yoḥanan, with regard to non-sacred land; and Rabbi Yona said [it] in the name of Rabbi Yoḥanan with regard to consecrated property.
rashi:b1.2: They are not subject to exploitation, but they are subject to nullification of a transaction: that if he was wronged by more than one-sixth, he may retract. According to Rabbi Yona, [one statement of] Rabbi Yoḥanan contradicts [another statement of] Rabbi Yoḥanan.
rashi:b2.1: Reverse: Rabbi Yoḥanan said that one is required to conduct an appraisal by Torah law, and Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish said by rabbinic law.
rashi:b3.1: This works out well: according to Rabbi Yona, who said that Rabbi Yoḥanan said with regard to consecrated property that it is subject to nullification of a transaction, even though “his brother” is written, and all the more so with regard to lands, what you reversed works out well.
rashi:b4.1: But according to Rabbi Yirmeya: if you reverse it, [one statement of] Rabbi Yoḥanan contradicts [another statement of] Rabbi Yoḥanan.
rashi:b5.1: Rabbi Yirmeya could say to you: Do not reverse: [Rashi’s text reads “Rabbi Yirmeya could say to you,” where ours reads “Rabbi Yirmeya said.”] For it certainly is as was said at first, and Rabbi Yona answers according to his own reasoning and reverses it.
rashi:b7.1: No, both this Sage and that Sage hold in accordance with Shmuel: and if he intends to desacralize it [for less], it is certainly desacralized; that is, if it was in his mind to wrong the consecrated property and desacralize it for less money, it is certainly desacralized. But Reish Lakish said that one is required to conduct an appraisal by Torah law for this reason: because he did not intend to desacralize it for less money, but thought that the non-sacred animal was worth the value of the consecrated one; and Rabbi Yoḥanan holds that even so he intends to desacralize it.
rashi:b8.1: And if you wish, say: even according to Rabbi Yona, do not reverse this [dispute] of Rabbi Yoḥanan and Reish Lakish. They are dealing with exploitation, and did not speak of nullification of a transaction at all. And as for the difficulty for Reish Lakish from the mishna “These are matters,” it is not difficult, for Reish Lakish explains it in accordance with Rav Ḥisda: that even [a disparity of] less than one-sixth is returned. This is what the verse “a man [to] his brother” is saying: it is [there] that he pays a disparity of one-sixth, and less than one-sixth he does not pay; but with consecrated property, even less than the measure of exploitation is returned. And this is the “by Torah law” that Reish Lakish said above. And Rabbi Yoḥanan understands [the mishna] according to its plain meaning. But Rabbi Yoḥanan did not speak of nullification of a transaction at all, and there is no difficulty, either for Rabbi Yoḥanan or for Rabbi Yirmeya.
rashi:b10.1: They said only: that a layman pays the consecrated property the entire disparity, only where two assessed it at first and erred, and then three returned and assessed it higher for the consecrated property.
rashi:b10.2: But where three assessed it: at first, even if a hundred come back and say that the first ones erred, the assessment is not reversed.
rashi:b12.1: And even three and three: [Rashi’s text reads “And even,” where ours reads “And furthermore.”] That is, even if only three came and contradicted the first three, the hand of the consecrated property is uppermost and we follow the latter ones.
rashi:b14.1: Mishna. This one in place of this sin offering: that the sin offering was standing before him.
rashi:b15.1: These are hereby for a burnt offering: [this] implies for the value of a burnt offering, for if he had wanted to sacrifice them themselves, he would have said: These are hereby a burnt offering.
rashi:b16.1: Gemara. The mishna: which teaches “in place of a sin offering, in place of a burnt offering, he has said nothing,” is not in accordance with Rabbi Meir, who says [of one who pledged the valuation of an infant less than a month old] that he gives its value, as much as it is fit to be sold for in the market; for a person knows that there is no valuation for one less than a month old, and he resolved and spoke for the sake of [its] value.
rashi:b17.1: They do not require a blemish: they do not require grazing, for they are already standing disqualified.
rashi:b17.2: But one who separates a female, etc., requires a blemish: since it is fit to be sacrificed as a peace offering.
rashi:b18.1: Not in accordance with Rabbi Shimon: who says in the chapter Elu Kodashim (above, Temurah 19b): One who separates a female for a guilt offering, it is sold without a blemish. Another version: [the mishna implies that a female designated for a burnt offering] is itself sacred, so that it requires grazing; [this is] not in accordance with Rabbi Shimon, who says in the chapter Elu Kodashim: even for his burnt offering it does not render a substitute, which shows that it itself does not become sacred.
tosafot:b7.1: In brief: Tosafot quotes Rashi’s explanation [that if he meant to wrong the Temple and desacralize the property for less, it is certainly desacralized, while Reish Lakish requires an appraisal by Torah law because the owner thought the non-sacred animal was worth as much as the consecrated one, and Rabbi Yoḥanan holds that even so he means to desacralize it]. Accordingly they explain the wording: “When Shmuel stated it, after the fact” means a case that is permitted not ab initio but only after the fact, where he intentionally desacralized it for less than its value; “but not ab initio” means a case that is permitted ab initio, where he did not intend to lower its value but thought the non-sacred was worth as much as the consecrated and erred, and there Shmuel did not say that the sanctity transfers. Rabbi Yirmeya holds that Shmuel said it is desacralized even in that case. One cannot explain at face value that Shmuel said it is desacralized after the fact but not that one may do so ab initio: for then Rabbi Yoḥanan’s statement that they are not subject to exploitation but are subject to nullification would be speaking ab initio, and is one permitted to wrong consecrated property ab initio? Further, how could Rabbi Yirmeya say that Shmuel permits desacralizing property worth a maneh on a peruta’s worth even ab initio? Further, Shmuel’s word “is desacralized” itself implies after the fact. And further, the first chapter of Sanhedrin (14b) says that redeeming consecrated property requires nine Israelites and one priest, derived there from verses. Therefore one must explain as Rashi did. Open on Sefaria for the full text.
tosafot:b10.1: In brief: “They said only where two assessed it” refers to what was said, that even less than the measure of exploitation is returned: the layman returns the shortfall to the Temple, yet the desacralization stands. The difficulty: the chapter HaNeḥnakin (Sanhedrin 88a), on the rebellious elder, implies that even a drainpipe of consecrated property requires ten people to redeem it. It establishes there that the elder and the Sanhedrin disagree as in the dispute of Rabbi Eliezer and the Rabbis about the assessment of consecrated property, since the elder is liable only for a matter that carries liability for a sin offering: if the property was redeemed by three, according to Rabbi Eliezer it is not redeemed and remains consecrated, so that if one afterward betrothed a woman with it she is not betrothed, while according to the Rabbis it is redeemed and goes out to non-sacred status, and she is betrothed. Evidently three, or ten, each according to his view, are indispensable, yet here it implies that it is desacralized by two. Further, how could Shmuel say it is desacralized on a peruta’s worth? One must say that here it speaks of an owner redeeming his own consecrated property, and in such a case Shmuel said it is desacralized for less than its value; but a treasurer selling consecrated property requires three or ten, each according to his view. Open on Sefaria for the full text.
tosafot:b16.1: The mishna is not in accordance with Rabbi Meir: that is, [the clause] that teaches “in place of a sin offering, in place of a burnt offering, he has said nothing”; for since Rabbi Meir says that a person does not utter his words for naught, so too here his intention was for the sin offering that he has at home or the burnt offering that he has at home. And some also explain that it refers to what it teaches: if he said about a non-kosher animal and about a blemished animal “These are hereby a burnt offering,” he has said nothing. This is not in accordance with Rabbi Meir, for since a person does not utter his words for naught, his intention was to say “for a burnt offering,” and he resolved and spoke for the sake of [its] value.
gershom:b1.1: Rather, where they erred by the measure of nullification of a transaction, more than one-sixth: in this case would Rabbi Yoḥanan say it is by rabbinic law and not by Torah law? But it was stated: Rabbi Yona said with regard to consecrated property this which it goes on to say below, that they are subject to nullification of a transaction by Torah law.
gershom:b2.1: And Rabbi Yirmeya said with regard to land that they are subject to nullification of a transaction, and both said in the name of Rabbi Yoḥanan: they are subject to nullification of a transaction, by Torah law.
gershom:b3.1: And reverse: Rabbi Yoḥanan, who said by rabbinic law, explain him as Reish Lakish, and Reish Lakish as Rabbi Yoḥanan, and it is not difficult for you.
gershom:b4.1: But can you say reverse? This works out well according to the one who says that Rabbi Yoḥanan said that consecrated property is subject to nullification of a transaction, and all the more so with regard to land; it was necessary to say reverse. But according to Rabbi Yirmeya, land is subject to nullification of a transaction and not consecrated property; how can he reverse it?
gershom:b5.1: Rather, do not reverse: and Rabbi Yoḥanan says that they are subject to nullification of a transaction by rabbinic law and not by Torah law, according to the words of Rabbi Yirmeya.
gershom:b6.1: Shall we say that they disagree: Rabbi Yona and Rabbi Yirmeya, with regard to Shmuel’s [statement], as Shmuel said: Consecrated property worth a maneh that one desacralized onto a peruta’s worth is desacralized.
gershom:b7.1: That Rabbi Yona does not hold in accordance with Shmuel: for he holds that they are subject to nullification of a transaction, and this one, who desacralized it onto a peruta, [is] more than nullification of a transaction. And Rabbi Yirmeya does hold [in accordance with Shmuel].
gershom:b8.1: And if you wish, say: Actually, as was said at first, that they disagree with regard to exploitation, a disparity of one-sixth, and do not reverse. As for what is difficult for Reish Lakish, “These are matters that are not subject to exploitation: consecrated property,” he holds that they are not subject to exploitation as Rav Ḥisda explains, that even less than the measure of exploitation is returned. Another version: With regard to what do Rabbi Yoḥanan and Reish Lakish disagree? With regard to Shmuel’s [statement]. According to Rabbi Yoḥanan, who said both this and that are by Torah law, he does not hold in accordance with Shmuel, as we answered “reverse.” And if you wish, say: even Rav [the text reads “Rav,” perhaps for Reish Lakish] holds in accordance with Shmuel, and he could say to you: if he intends ab initio to desacralize it thus, onto a peruta’s worth, it is properly desacralized; but here in the mishna it is different, with one who says “This is desacralized onto this,” who does not intend to desacralize it for a peruta. Therefore it says that he must conduct an appraisal by Torah law.
gershom:b9.1: And if you wish, say: no one holds in accordance with Shmuel, and they disagree with regard to the measure of exploitation, etc.
gershom:b10.1: They taught only: that he must conduct an appraisal, so that the consecrated property should not be wronged, only where the consecrated property was not assessed by three when he said “This is desacralized onto this”; but if it was assessed by three, it is not reversed, and he need not conduct an appraisal again.
gershom:b11.1: But didn’t Rav Safra say: Where does one say that a hundred witnesses are like two? That is, [if] a hundred witnesses contradict two witnesses, these two are considered like those hundred, for we do not believe these more than those, since they do not render them conspiring witnesses.
gershom:b12.1: But with regard to assessment we follow the majority of opinions: even though it was assessed by three at first.
gershom:b13.1: And furthermore, even if there were only three and three, and the latter three add to the assessment, don’t we follow the latter? Rather, Ulla, who said that if it was assessed by three it is not reversed, holds in accordance with Rabbi Yoḥanan, etc.
gershom:b14.1: Another version: We said that he must conduct an appraisal again only where it was assessed at first by two; but where it was assessed by three, even if a hundred come and add, it is not reversed. And one should not say that the assessment of these three should be no better than that of two, so that if others come and add it should be reversed; it teaches us that it is not reversed, since it was assessed by three. [The printed text adds a garbled phrase: “But didn’t Rav Safra say: even according to the one who says, etc.”]
gershom:b15.1: This is hereby in place of a sin offering, or in place of a burnt offering, and he has neither a sin offering nor a burnt offering: he has still said nothing.
gershom:b16.1: [And if he said]: in place of a sin offering, or in place of a sin offering that he has in his house, his statement stands.
gershom:b17.1: For if [it were] Rabbi Meir, didn’t he say: A person does not utter his words for naught, and he resolved and spoke for the sake of its value? Here too he would hold that it is sold.
gershom:b18.1: The reason is that he said it about a non-kosher animal and about a blemished animal: they are sold at once [the text adds the unclear words “without his intent”], because they are already standing disqualified; but one who separates a female for a guilt offering requires a blemish before it is sold.
gershom:b19.1: Another version: But if he said about a female “This is hereby for a burnt offering,” it is consecrated with inherent sanctity as a burnt offering, and it is sold, and it renders a substitute, since its body is fit [to be sacrificed] as a peace offering.
gershom:b20.1: And not in accordance with Rabbi Shimon ben Yehuda [Rabbeinu Gershom’s text reads Rabbi Shimon ben Yehuda, where ours reads Rabbi Shimon], who said above in the chapter Elu Kodashim: even for a burnt offering they do not render a substitute, for he does not accept the reasoning of “since,” and does not hold that the name “burnt offering” [applies] to its mother.
gershom:b21.1: Hadran alakh Keitzad Ma’arimin: we will return to you, “How One Employs Artifice.”
